     22	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     23	
     24	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     25	
     26	## When to Use This Skill
     27	
     28	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     29	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     30	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     31	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots are safe to delete.
     32	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     33	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     34	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     35	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     36	
     37	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     38	
     39	## Prerequisites
     40	
     41	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     42	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     43	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     44	
     45	---
     46	
     47	## Workflow
     48	
     49	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     50	
     51	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     52	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     53	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     54	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     55	
     56	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     57	
     58	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     59	|---|---|---|
     60	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     61	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     62	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     63	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     64	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     65	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     66	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     67	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     68	
     69	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     70	
     71	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     72	
     73	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     74	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     75	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     76	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     77	
     78	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     79	
     80	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     81	
     82	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     83	
     84	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     85	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     86	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, or Not applicable.
     87	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     88	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     89	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     90	
     91	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every review answer starts with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`.
     92	
     93	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     94	
     95	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     96	
     97	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     98	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom.
     99	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     100	- Every "safe to delete" verdict is backed by the checks its tier requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not safe to delete.
     101	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     102	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     103

     105	
     106	## Critical Rules
     107	
     108	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, DeleteSnapshot, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     109	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     110	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     111	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     112	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     113	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     114	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     115	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. AWS CloudTrail is optional; `DescribeVolumesModifications` is the change record.
     116	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     117	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     118	
     119	## Error Handling
     120	
     121	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.

{"id": "4490e32b-794d-49da-ba8e-02a1104885cf", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_nhgpsUlpM3sWMwihCvHQPF", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history (when it first entered ALARM).
     17	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     18	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     19	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     20	
     21	### Step 2: Build the context
     22	
     23	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).
     24	- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.
     25	- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.
     26	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).
     27	- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence. An impaired status or a failing check is a scope signal for escalation (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)), but still finish Steps 3 to 5.
     28	
     29	### Step 2b: Rule EBS in or out (chat requests with no EBS alarm only)
     30	
     31	This check runs only when the run did not start from an AWS/EBS alarm or an `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` alarm, for example a chat request such as "my app is slow, is it storage?". When an EBS alarm triggered the run, skip this step and run Steps 3 to 6 in full.
     32	
     33	Read `CPUUtilization` for the instance, and the latency, `VolumeQueueLength`, `BurstBalance` (gp2, st1, sc1) and instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` (if published) for the volumes found in Step 2, over the same window. Use the qualitative attribution matrix in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). Report "Not EBS" and stop tuning storage only if all of these hold: CPU is high, volume latency and queue length are normal, no `DescribeVolumeStatus` problem was found, and no burst or instance balance is draining or at 0. Otherwise continue with Step 3.
     34	
     35	### Step 3: Measure each volume on the dimension(s) its type is limited by
     36	
     37	Pull the last 30 minutes of AWS/EBS metrics at 1-minute granularity.
     38	
     39	- Actual IOPS = (VolumeReadOps + VolumeWriteOps) / period seconds
     40	- Actual throughput = (VolumeReadBytes + VolumeWriteBytes) / period, in MiB/s
     41	- Avg latency = VolumeTotalRead/WriteTime / ops; VolumeQueueLength
     42	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both dimensions, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 for MiB/s. `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only. If `VolumeAvg*` returns nothing, use the Sum-based math above.
     43	- Always read `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds in the period with no read or write submitted; `VolumeId` only). Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period seconds x 100. Report it as evidence for every volume. Near 0 means I/O was submitted for the whole period, which fits both saturation and impairment, so use Step 5 to tell them apart. A volume that is mostly idle during the alarm window is unlikely to be the binding volume. There is no fixed band; compare with the volume's own history.
     44	
     45	Apply the rule for the volume's type:
     46	
     47	- gp3: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently. Compare actual IOPS to Iops AND actual MiB/s to Throughput; either can bind.
     48	- gp2: baseline IOPS = 3 x GiB (min 100), burst to 3,000 while BurstBalance > 0. Check BurstBalance draining or at 0.
     49	- io1/io2 (incl. Block Express): compare actual IOPS to provisioned Iops. Throughput is derived from IOPS x I/O size, not provisioned separately. Do NOT use VolumeThroughputPercentage to judge throughput on io1/io2; it reports the % of provisioned IOPS delivered.
     50	- st1/sc1: throughput-oriented with burst credits; compare MiB/s to the baseline/burst for the size and check BurstBalance.
     51	- Judge io2 by IOPS; judge gp3 by throughput and IOPS. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     52	
     53	### Step 4: Check the instance layer
     54	
     55	- Sum actual IOPS and MiB/s across all attached volumes; compare to the instance type's EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes.
     56	- Aggregate across ALL attached volumes, including the root volume.
     57	- Check EBSIOBalance% / EBSByteBalance%. If they are draining or at 0, or the sum is at the instance limit, the INSTANCE is the binding layer and raising volume provisioning will not help.
     58	- If instance metrics are healthy and a volume is at its own limit, the VOLUME is the binding layer.
     59	- If `EBSIOBalance%` is absent, the instance size does not publish it. Use the summed values against the baseline.
     60	
     61	### Step 5: Distinguish saturation from impairment
     62	
     63	If queue length and latency are elevated but the volume and instance are both below their limits, this is NOT saturation. Suspect an impairment or injected latency; do NOT recommend increasing provisioning.
     64	
     65	The impairment signature is IOPS and throughput collapsing while latency and `VolumeQueueLength` rise. Saturation looks different: metrics flat at the provisioned limit with modest latency. When you see the impairment signature, check in this order:
     66	
     67	1. The `DescribeVolumeStatus` result from Step 2 (impaired status, failing checks, scheduled events). Read it again if the symptom started after Step 2.
     68	2. AWS Health `DescribeEvents` for Amazon EBS and Amazon EC2 events in the Region and Availability Zone.
     69	3. AWS FIS `ListExperiments` for a running experiment that targets the volume or instance, with actions `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` or `aws:ebs:pause-volume-io`. If one is running, say so plainly: the latency is injected and will end with the experiment.
     70
